name: Samburu
confidence_why: Dahlbacka 2014, the only first-hand phonology of Samburu, finds stress non-contrastive and assigned from the tone pattern, and Heine 1980 describes the same tone-driven accent for the neighbouring Chamus dialect, the two differing only on which high tone is prominent in an all-high word.

catalog_quote: Stress is not contrastive in Samburu. There are two simple rules for stress assignment, that involve a combination of tone pattern and position of the syllable in the word. As stress and tone interact it is important to listen to the tone pattern of a word if one wants to determine where the stress falls. The stress placement rules operate in phonological words, which include any proclitic (genitive particle, te/tɛ, ɛɪtʊ́). ... High tone attracts stress. Relevance: other language; priority none. The folder already held, from an earlier reading today, the best first-hand statement: Dahlbacka 2014, A Phonological Description of the Samburu Language (BTL Kenya, open PDF from Webonary), ch. 6 'Stress rules' pp. 66-68, read in full held by the project: stress is non-contrastive and predictable from tone (sole H; else last H before L / final syllable of all-H words / falling-tone syllable; first H after initial L's), weight-insensitive, realised by extra pitch and sometimes duration; she departs from Heine 1980:103-104 (Chamus 'Note on accent', reconstructed only from archive.org snippets, lending-only, priority medium) and the unobtained Wagner 1997 BTL ms. new_statements.quote: Stress is not contrastive in Samburu. [...] High tone attracts stress. This means that if a word has only one high tone, that syllable will be stressed [...] a) If a word has only high tones, the last syllable will be stressed. [...] b) If there is a series of high tones followed by one or several low tones, the last high tone is stressed. c) If a low tone intervenes between two high tones, the second high tone is stressed. d) If there is a falling tone, it is the stressed syllable. [...] The second stress rule says that if a word starts with one or several low tones, and is followed by several high tones, the first high tone will be stressed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Samburu is a tone language (surface H, L and word-final falling; underlyingly H vs L, lexical and grammatical). Word stress is non-contrastive and fully predictable from the tone pattern of the phonological word: a word's sole H-toned syllable is stressed; in an all-H word the final syllable; where a run of H tones is followed by L(s), the last H; where L intervenes between two H, the second H; a (word-final) falling-tone syllable is always the stressed one (consistent with 'last H' if falling = HL on one mora); but if the word begins with L(s) followed by several H, the FIRST H is stressed (the L-to-H contour attracts prominence). Stress is realised as extra pitch height and sometimes extra duration; syllable weight (closed syllables, complex nuclei) plays no role.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; no secondary stress described.
new_statements.exceptions: A few function words ([aa] 'which', [ʄa] 'just', [koɾe]) carry only low tones and never occur in isolation (fn. 40) -- no stress rule given for all-L words. Author notes (fn. 77) her rules differ from Wagner 1997:7-8, who followed Heine 1980:103-104 (Chamus: accent on high-falling syllable, else sole H, else last H before L / usually first H otherwise). Rule (a)-(d) vs the 'second rule' are stated as environment-specific, not exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Rules operate in the phonological word, which includes proclitics (genitive particle, te/tɛ, ɛɪtʊ́) (p. 66, citing Wagner 1997:7). Evidence from auditory impression plus measurements on recorded sound files (isolation/citation forms and short verb phrases in the tables). Variety: Samburu proper (Samburu County); author reports no major internal dialect differences; data largely from Wagner's c.1997 wordlist re-checked with named Samburu speakers; sketch checked by Doris Payne.
new_statements.identity_note: Dahlbacka 2014 describes Samburu proper (saq, samb1315; Samburu County, Kenya; author reports no major internal dialects). The parallel older statement in Heine 1980 §2.14 concerns Chamus/Ilchamus (Glottolog dialect cham1311 under samb1315) and says the same non-distinctive, tone-determined accent holds 'like in the other Maa dialects'. Lentete 2016 (Ilchamus) is segmental only.

new_statements.quote: Stress is not contrastive in Samburu. There are two simple rules for stress assignment, that involve a combination of tone pattern and position of the syllable in the word. [...] High tone attracts stress. This means that if a word has only one high tone, that syllable will be stressed [...] The first stress rule say that the last high tone will be stressed in the following environments: a) If a word has only high tones, the last syllable will be stressed. b) If there is a series of high tones followed by one or several low tones, the last high tone is stressed. c) If a low tone intervenes between two high tones, the second high tone is stressed. d) If there is a falling tone, it is the stressed syllable. [...] The second stress rule says that if a word starts with one or several low tones, and is followed by several high tones, the first high tone will be stressed. [...] Heavy syllables do not play a role in stress assignment
new_statements.citation: Dahlbacka, Anna. 2014. A Phonological Description of the Samburu Language. Nairobi: Bible Translation & Literacy (E.A.). Ch. 6 'Stress rules', pp. 66-68.

new_statements.reading: Samburu word stress is non-contrastive and entirely tone-conditioned (no fixed edge, no weight sensitivity): the sole H syllable, otherwise the last H before a following L / the final syllable of an all-H word / the falling-tone syllable, except that after an initial run of L's the first H of a following H-run is stressed. Phonetically extra pitch height, sometimes extra duration. The author (BTL, first-hand fieldwork with recordings) notes her rules differ from Wagner 1997 and Heine 1980:103-104. For a catalog this reads as 'stress predictable from tone / tone-driven prominence' rather than a positional stress system.

[...] (1) The accent is placed on the syllable carrying a high-falling tone. (2) If the word does not contain a high-falling tone then the accent is placed on a high tone syll- able subject to the following conditions: (a) If the word contains only one high tone then it is that syllable carrying the high tone which re- ceives the accent; (b) If there is a sequence of high tones then the accent is placed on the last high tone syllable if a low tone follows and usually on the first high tone syllable otherwise.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog (Dahlbacka 2014: stress non-contrastive, predictable from tone) and the same placement for a sole H, for an H-run followed by L (last H) and for a falling-tone syllable. It differs in one sub-case: for H-runs not followed by a low tone (all-H words) Heine puts the accent 'usually on the first high tone syllable', whereas Dahlbacka 2014 rule a) stresses the LAST syllable of an all-H word (Table 82, p. 67) and reserves first-H stress for words beginning with one or more low tones (her second rule, pp. 67-68). Dahlbacka fn. 77 states outright that she reaches 'different conclusions than Wagner 1997:7-8 (who in turn has borrowed his stress rules from Heine 1980:103-104)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is non-distinctive and entirely tone-driven: it falls on the high-falling-tone syllable if there is one; otherwise on a high-tone syllable -- the sole H if there is only one, and in a run of H's the last H when a low tone follows, 'usually' the first H of the run otherwise. No edge or weight condition; accent is left unmarked in the sketch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the recovered text.
new_statements.exceptions: Rule (2b) is hedged with 'usually' for H-runs not followed by a low tone. A later snippet (sect. 2.14, examples) says certain prefixes 'show a variable tone/accent behaviour themselves but they determine tone and accent of the following syllable in a predictable way', e.g. the person markers.
new_statements.identity_note: Heine 1980 describes Camus (Il-Chamus, Njemps), which Glottolog 5.1 lists as the dialect cham1311 under Samburu samb1315 and which Heine's bib entry codes as 'Camus = Samburu [saq]'; Heine presents its accent as behaving 'like in the other Maa dialects'. Dahlbacka 2014 describes Samburu proper (she treats Samburu as a language and notes that Lewis 2013 lists Ilchamus as a dialect of it). The accent rules in the catalog therefore come from two sister North Maa varieties, not one. Park & Bucholtz 2009 is a Glottolog machine misattribution (keyword 'transcripts') with no connection to any Maa variety.

readall_conflicts: One real disagreement, already flagged by the primary source itself. Heine 1980 (Camus dialect, sect. 2.14, p. 103) and Dahlbacka 2014 (Samburu, ch. 6, pp. 66-68) agree that the accent/stress is non-distinctive and assigned from the tone pattern, and agree on three sub-cases (sole H; H-run followed by L -> last H; falling-tone syllable). They differ on H-runs with no following low tone: Heine says the accent goes 'usually on the first high tone syllable otherwise', Dahlbacka says the last syllable of an all-H word is stressed (rule a, Table 82) and stresses the first H only after an initial run of low tones. Dahlbacka fn. 77 states that her instrumental and auditory analysis leads to 'different conclusions than Wagner 1997:7-8 (who in turn has borrowed his stress rules from Heine 1980:103-104)'. Part of the gap may be dialectal (Camus vs Samburu proper) and Heine's rule is hedged with 'usually'. Park & Bucholtz 2009 is not a source on this language and creates no conflict.

sources.quote: Camus has an accent which, like in the other Maa dialects, has no distinctive function and will not be marked in the present paper. The following general rules can be established for the placement of the word accent: (1) The accent is placed on the syllable carrying a high-falling tone. (2) If the word does not contain a high-falling tone then the accent is placed on a high tone syllable subject to the following conditions: (a) If the word contains only one high tone then it is that syllable carrying the high tone which receives the accent; (b) If there is a sequence of high tones then the accent is placed on the last high tone syllable if a low tone follows and usually on the first high tone syllable otherwise.
